fields.Question: Adding more CPU, memory or disk to a single machine is called what?
fields.Hint: Think of growing one box taller rather than adding boxes.
fields.Fact: Vertical scaling is eventually capped by the largest machine you can buy.

fields.Question: Adding more machines to share the load is called what?
fields.Hint: Think of adding boxes side by side.
fields.Fact: Horizontal scaling usually works best when the service tier is stateless.

fields.Text: A {{c1::stateless}} service keeps no client session data between requests, so any instance can handle any request.
fields.Extra: Session state is moved to a shared store such as a database or cache.
fields.Hint: It is the property that makes instances interchangeable.
fields.Fact: Stateless instances can be added or removed behind a load balancer without draining sessions.

fields.Text: {{c1::Amdahl's law}} says the speedup from parallelism is limited by the fraction of the work that must stay serial.
fields.Extra: If 5% of a task is serial, the speedup can never exceed 20x, no matter how many processors you add.
fields.Hint: Named after an IBM computer architect.
fields.Fact: Gene Amdahl presented the argument at the 1967 AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference.
fields.Source: Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities (https://doi.org/10.1145/1465482.1465560)

fields.Text: Little's law: average items in a system L equals arrival rate {{c1::lambda}} times average time in the system {{c2::W}}.
fields.Extra: Example: 100 requests per second at 0.2 s each means about 20 requests in flight.
fields.Hint: It relates concurrency, throughput and latency.
fields.Fact: John Little published a proof of the formula in 1961.
fields.Source: A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = lambda W (https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383)

fields.Question: A service gets 500 requests per second and each takes 0.1 s. By Little's law, how many requests are in flight on average?
fields.Hint: Multiply arrival rate by time in system.
fields.Fact: Little's law holds for any stable system regardless of the arrival distribution.
fields.Source: A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = lambda W (https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383)

fields.Side B: Routes by IP address and TCP or UDP port without reading the request content
fields.Hint: Think of the transport layer of the OSI model.
fields.Fact: Because it does not parse HTTP, an L4 balancer cannot route by URL path.

fields.Side B: Routes using application data such as HTTP host, path or headers
fields.Aliases:
L7 load balancer
Application load balancer
fields.Hint: Think of the application layer of the OSI model.
fields.Fact: An L7 balancer typically terminates the client connection and opens its own connection to the backend.

fields.Question: Which load balancing method sends each new request to the next server in a fixed rotation?
fields.Hint: It ignores how busy each server is.
fields.Fact: Round robin is the default method in NGINX upstream groups.

fields.Question: Which load balancing method sends a request to the server with the fewest active connections?
fields.Hint: It adapts to requests of uneven duration.
fields.Fact: NGINX enables this method with the least_conn directive.

fields.Question: Which load balancing method picks a server from a hash of the client address, so a client keeps hitting the same server?
fields.Fact: Clients behind one shared NAT address all land on the same backend with this method.

fields.Question: Which load balancing method rotates through servers but gives bigger servers proportionally more turns?
fields.Hint: A plain rotation plus a per server number.
fields.Fact: Weights let mixed hardware share one pool without overloading the smaller machines.

fields.Text: Load balancers use {{c1::health checks}} to stop sending traffic to instances that fail a probe.
fields.Extra: Active checks probe an endpoint periodically. Passive checks watch real traffic for failures.
fields.Hint: The balancer asks each backend whether it is alive.
fields.Fact: A health endpoint that checks every dependency can take the whole fleet out of rotation when one shared dependency fails.

fields.Text: {{c1::Sticky sessions}} (session affinity) route all requests from one client to the same backend instance.
fields.Extra: Often implemented with a load balancer cookie.
fields.Hint: The client keeps returning to one instance.
fields.Fact: Affinity can unbalance load and loses the session if that instance dies.

fields.Text: With {{c1::anycast}} routing, many servers in different places announce the same IP address and the network delivers packets to a nearby one.
fields.Extra: Widely used by CDNs and DNS resolvers.
fields.Fact: Anycast relies on BGP route selection, so nearest means nearest by routing, not always by distance.

fields.Text: Adding {{c1::read replicas}} scales read throughput, but reads from them may return stale data because of {{c2::replication lag}}.
fields.Extra: Writes still go to the leader.
fields.Hint: Copies of the database that serve queries.
fields.Fact: With asynchronous replication, a replica can fall seconds or more behind the leader under load.

fields.Text: {{c1::Sharding}} splits a dataset across multiple databases so that each holds a subset of the rows.
fields.Extra: Also called horizontal partitioning.
fields.Fact: A good shard key spreads both data and traffic evenly.

fields.Question: A shard that gets far more traffic than the others, for example because one celebrity key lives there, is called what?
fields.Hint: It is about skew, not total volume.
fields.Fact: Adding a random suffix to a very hot key spreads its writes across shards, at the cost of fan-in reads.

fields.Question: Which partitioning scheme keeps keys sorted so range scans are efficient, but risks hot spots on sequential keys?
fields.Aliases:
Key range partitioning
Range based partitioning
fields.Hint: Think of an encyclopedia split by letter.
fields.Fact: Bigtable partitions tables into row ranges called tablets.
fields.Source: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data (https://research.google/pubs/bigtable-a-distributed-storage-system-for-structured-data/)

fields.Text: With simple hash(key) mod N placement, changing N moves {{c1::most}} keys to a different node.
fields.Extra: This is the problem consistent hashing solves.
fields.Hint: Think about what happens to every remainder when the divisor changes.
fields.Fact: Going from 4 to 5 nodes with mod hashing keeps only about 1 in 5 keys in place.

fields.Text: In {{c1::consistent hashing}}, nodes and keys are hashed onto a ring and each key belongs to the next node clockwise.
fields.Extra: Adding or removing a node only moves the keys in its neighbouring arc.
fields.Hint: Imagine a circle of hash values.
fields.Fact: Karger and colleagues introduced it in 1997 to manage web caches.

fields.Text: When a node joins a consistent hash ring of N nodes holding K keys, on average about {{c1::K/N}} keys move.
fields.Extra: Compare with mod N hashing, where most keys move.
fields.Hint: Only one share of the keyspace changes owner.
fields.Fact: This minimal movement is why caches can grow without a mass of cold misses.

fields.Question: What technique places each physical server at many points on a consistent hash ring to even out load?
fields.Hint: Each server gets many tokens, not one.
fields.Fact: Dynamo used virtual nodes so a node's share can match its capacity.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Question: Which alternative to the hash ring scores every node for a key and picks the highest score?
fields.Aliases:
Highest random weight hashing
HRW hashing
HRW
fields.Hint: Each node's score comes from hashing the key together with the node.
fields.Fact: Rendezvous hashing needs no ring structure, at the cost of scoring every node per lookup.

fields.Text: Google's {{c1::jump consistent hash}} maps a key to one of N numbered buckets with no ring and almost no memory.
fields.Extra: It suits data stores where buckets are numbered sequentially, not arbitrary node sets.
fields.Hint: Its name describes how the bucket index moves forward.
fields.Fact: Lamping and Veach published it in 2014; the core is only a few lines of code.
fields.Source: A Fast, Minimal Memory, Consistent Hash Algorithm (https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.2294)

fields.Side B: Stops calling a failing dependency for a while and fails fast instead
fields.Hint: Named after an electrical safety device.
fields.Fact: A half open state lets a few trial calls through to test whether the dependency recovered.

fields.Side B: Isolates resources such as thread pools per dependency so one failure cannot exhaust them all
fields.Hint: Named after watertight compartments in a ship.
fields.Fact: Separate connection pools per downstream service are a common bulkhead.

fields.Text: Retrying with exponential backoff plus random {{c1::jitter}} prevents many clients from retrying in lockstep.
fields.Extra: AWS found full jitter greatly reduced total work compared with backoff alone.
fields.Hint: A little randomness in the wait time.
fields.Fact: Without jitter, clients that failed together retry together and can overload the service again.

fields.Text: {{c1::Load shedding}} deliberately rejects some requests when a server is overloaded so it can keep serving the rest.
fields.Extra: Cheap rejections, such as an early 503, protect latency for accepted requests.
fields.Hint: Dropping part of the load on purpose.
fields.Fact: The Google SRE book recommends that servers protect themselves from overload rather than relying only on clients.

fields.Question: In which caching pattern does the application check the cache, and on a miss read the database and populate the cache itself?
fields.Hint: The cache sits beside the data path, not in it.
fields.Fact: Cache-aside only caches data that is actually requested.

fields.Question: In which caching pattern is every write sent to the cache and the backing store synchronously?
fields.Hint: The write passes through the cache on its way down.
fields.Fact: It keeps the cache fresh but adds write latency.

fields.Question: In which caching pattern are writes acknowledged once in the cache and flushed to the store later?
fields.Fact: If the cache node fails before flushing, those writes can be lost.

fields.Question: In which caching pattern do writes go straight to the store and skip the cache entirely?
fields.Hint: The write goes past the cache.
fields.Fact: It avoids filling the cache with data that may never be read.

fields.Question: In which caching pattern does the cache itself load missing data from the store, so the app only talks to the cache?
fields.Hint: The cache does the lookup on a miss.
fields.Fact: Compared with cache-aside, the loading logic moves from the application into the cache layer.

fields.Side B: Evicts the entry that has gone the longest without being accessed
fields.Fact: A hash map plus a doubly linked list gives O(1) LRU get and put.

fields.Side B: Evicts the entry with the fewest accesses
fields.Fact: Plain LFU can keep once popular items forever unless counts decay.

fields.Side B: Evicts the entry that was inserted earliest, regardless of use
fields.Fact: FIFO ignores hits entirely, which makes it simple and cheap.

fields.Question: Which theoretical eviction policy removes the item that will be needed furthest in the future?
fields.Hint: It needs to know the future, so it is only a benchmark.
fields.Fact: Laszlo Belady described it in 1966 while studying virtual memory replacement.
fields.Source: A study of replacement algorithms for a virtual-storage computer (https://doi.org/10.1147/sj.52.0078)

fields.Text: A {{c1::TTL}} (time to live) makes a cache entry expire automatically after a set duration.
fields.Extra: Short TTLs reduce staleness, long TTLs raise hit rate.
fields.Hint: A lifetime attached to each entry.
fields.Fact: Adding random jitter to TTLs keeps many keys from expiring at the same instant.

fields.Text: Redis does not implement exact LRU: it {{c1::samples}} a few keys and evicts the best candidate among them.
fields.Extra: The sample size is set by maxmemory-samples.
fields.Fact: Redis eviction policies include allkeys-lru, volatile-lru, allkeys-lfu and noeviction.

fields.Question: Which Redis maxmemory policy returns errors on writes instead of evicting anything?
fields.Hint: The name says what it does not do.
fields.Fact: With this policy, reads keep working when memory is full; commands that would add memory fail.

fields.Text: When a hot key expires and many requests miss at once and all hit the database, it is called a {{c1::cache stampede}}.
fields.Extra: Also known as the thundering herd or dog pile effect.
fields.Hint: Picture a herd charging the database together.
fields.Fact: Request coalescing lets one request rebuild the value while the others wait for it.

fields.Text: Caching the fact that a key does not exist is called {{c1::negative caching}}.
fields.Extra: It protects the store from repeated lookups for missing keys.
fields.Fact: Negative entries usually get a short TTL so newly created keys appear quickly.

fields.Text: A {{c1::Bloom filter}} can return false positives but never false negatives.
fields.Extra: Used to skip lookups for keys that are definitely absent.
fields.Hint: A bit array set by several hash functions.
fields.Fact: Burton Bloom described the structure in 1970.
fields.Source: Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/362686.362692)

fields.Text: A famous quip says the two hard things in computer science are {{c1::cache invalidation}} and naming things.
fields.Extra: Commonly attributed to Phil Karlton.
fields.Hint: One of them is about keeping copies correct.
fields.Fact: Variants of the joke add a third hard thing: off by one errors.

fields.Text: A {{c1::CDN}} serves content from edge servers close to users and fetches from the {{c2::origin}} on a miss.
fields.Extra: Content delivery network.
fields.Fact: Serving from the edge cuts round trip time and offloads traffic from the origin.
fields.Source: Cloudflare Learning: What is a CDN? (https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/cdn/what-is-a-cdn/)

fields.Text: In a {{c1::pull}} CDN, edges fetch from the origin on the first request; in a {{c2::push}} CDN, you upload content ahead of time.
fields.Extra: Pull is simpler, push suits large files that you know will be requested.
fields.Fact: Pull CDNs mean the first user in each region may see a slower cache miss.
fields.Source: Cloudflare Learning: What is a CDN? (https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/cdn/what-is-a-cdn/)

fields.Question: What metric is cache hits divided by total requests?
fields.Aliases:
Hit ratio
Hit rate
Cache hit rate
fields.Hint: A fraction of lookups that the cache answered.
fields.Fact: Raising a hit ratio from 90% to 99% cuts origin load by a factor of ten.
fields.Source: Cloudflare Learning: What is a CDN? (https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/cdn/what-is-a-cdn/)

fields.Question: Which Cache-Control directive gives the number of seconds a response stays fresh?
fields.Fact: Cache-Control: max-age=3600 means fresh for one hour.

fields.Question: Which Cache-Control directive sets freshness only for shared caches such as CDNs?
fields.Hint: It is a variant of the usual freshness directive with a prefix.
fields.Fact: For shared caches it overrides max-age and the Expires header.

fields.Side B: The response must not be stored by any cache
fields.Fact: no-cache, despite the name, allows storing but requires revalidation before each reuse.

fields.Side B: A cache may store the response but must revalidate it with the origin before each reuse
fields.Fact: no-cache combined with an ETag lets clients reuse content cheaply via 304 responses.

fields.Question: Which HTTP status code says a cached copy is still valid after a conditional request?
fields.Fact: A 304 response carries no body, which saves bandwidth.

fields.Text: A client revalidates using the {{c1::ETag}} it received by sending it back in an {{c2::If-None-Match}} header.
fields.Extra: If it still matches, the server replies 304 Not Modified.
fields.Hint: An entity tag is a version identifier for a representation.
fields.Fact: Weak ETags start with W/ and mean semantically equivalent rather than byte identical.

fields.Text: The {{c1::stale-while-revalidate}} directive lets a cache serve a stale response while it refreshes in the background.
fields.Extra: Defined in RFC 5861 along with stale-if-error.
fields.Hint: Serve old content now, fix it later.
fields.Fact: It hides refresh latency from users at the cost of briefly stale content.
fields.Source: RFC 5861: HTTP Cache-Control Extensions for Stale Content (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5861)

fields.Text: The {{c1::Vary}} response header tells caches which request headers change the response, so they store separate variants.
fields.Extra: Vary: Accept-Encoding is the classic example.
fields.Fact: Vary: User-Agent can fragment a CDN cache into many low hit variants.

fields.Text: Removing content from CDN edges before its TTL ends is called {{c1::purging}}.
fields.Extra: Also called invalidation.
fields.Hint: An explicit delete at the edge.
fields.Fact: Versioned file names, such as app.3f9a.js, avoid the need to purge static assets.
fields.Source: Cloudflare Learning: What is a CDN? (https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/cdn/what-is-a-cdn/)

fields.Text: The CAP theorem says that during a network {{c1::partition}}, a system must choose between {{c2::consistency}} and {{c3::availability}}.
fields.Extra: Gilbert and Lynch proved a formal version in 2002.
fields.Hint: Three letters, pick which one matters when the network splits.
fields.Fact: Eric Brewer first presented the idea as a conjecture at PODC in 2000.
fields.Source: Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/564585.564601)

fields.Text: PACELC extends CAP: if Partitioned, trade Availability against Consistency; Else, trade {{c1::latency}} against consistency.
fields.Extra: Proposed by Daniel Abadi.
fields.Hint: Even without a partition there is a cost to strong consistency.
fields.Fact: Abadi pointed out that the latency tradeoff applies all the time, not only during failures.
fields.Source: Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design (https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-pacelc.pdf)

fields.Question: Which consistency model makes every operation appear to take effect atomically at one instant between its start and end, respecting real time?
fields.Fact: Herlihy and Wing defined linearizability in 1990.

fields.Question: Which guarantee says concurrent transactions produce the same result as some serial order, without requiring that order to match real time?
fields.Hint: It is about transactions, not single objects.
fields.Fact: Strict serializability combines it with linearizability's real time ordering.

fields.Question: Which model only promises that replicas converge to the same value once updates stop?
fields.Fact: It says nothing about what reads return while updates are still flowing.

fields.Question: Which model guarantees that operations that are causally related are seen by everyone in the same order?
fields.Hint: Think of a reply never appearing before the message it answers.
fields.Fact: Jepsen lists causal consistency among models that can stay available during a partition if each client sticks to one server.

fields.Question: Which session guarantee ensures a user always sees their own earlier updates?
fields.Hint: Think of editing your profile and refreshing the page.
fields.Fact: A common implementation reads a user's own data from the leader for a short time after they write.

fields.Question: Which session guarantee ensures a user never sees data go back in time across successive reads?
fields.Hint: Think of a comment that appears, then vanishes on refresh.
fields.Fact: Routing each user to the same replica is one way to provide it.

fields.Text: With N replicas, a write quorum W and read quorum R, choosing {{c1::R + W > N}} ensures every read set overlaps the latest write set.
fields.Extra: Dynamo style systems make N, R and W configurable.
fields.Fact: A common configuration is N = 3, W = 2, R = 2.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Text: Dynamo used a {{c1::sloppy quorum}} with {{c2::hinted handoff}}: writes go to healthy nodes, which later pass the data to the intended node.
fields.Extra: This favours availability over strict quorum overlap.
fields.Hint: Stand in replicas hold a note about where the data belongs.
fields.Fact: Dynamo's paper describes this as being always writeable.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Question: What per replica counter vector did Dynamo use to detect concurrent, conflicting versions of an object?
fields.Fact: When two versions are concurrent, Dynamo returned both and let the application reconcile.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Question: Which logical clock, from a 1978 paper, gives every event a counter consistent with causality but cannot detect concurrency?
fields.Aliases:
Lamport timestamp
Lamport clocks
Logical clock
fields.Fact: The paper also introduced the happened before relation.
fields.Source: Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System (https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/time-clocks.pdf)

fields.Text: Google Spanner's {{c1::TrueTime}} API exposes clock uncertainty as an interval, and Spanner waits it out to give externally consistent transactions.
fields.Extra: It relies on GPS receivers and atomic clocks in datacenters.
fields.Hint: An honest clock that admits error bounds.
fields.Fact: The wait is called commit wait.

fields.Text: Dynamo replicas compare {{c1::Merkle trees}} to find which key ranges differ without transferring all the data.
fields.Extra: This background repair is called anti-entropy.
fields.Fact: Matching root hashes mean the whole range matches, so the comparison stops early.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Text: {{c1::Consensus}} lets a group of nodes agree on a single value, or a sequence of values, even if some nodes fail.
fields.Extra: Raft and Paxos are the classic algorithms.
fields.Hint: It is what a replicated log needs.
fields.Fact: Consensus is the basis of replicated state machines such as etcd and ZooKeeper.
fields.Source: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Text: The FLP result shows that no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee termination in a fully {{c1::asynchronous}} system if even one process may crash.
fields.Extra: Fischer, Lynch and Paterson, 1985.
fields.Hint: It is about systems without timing assumptions.
fields.Fact: Practical algorithms sidestep FLP with timeouts or randomization.
fields.Source: Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3149.214121)

fields.Question: A Raft or Paxos cluster of 5 servers can tolerate how many server failures and still make progress?
fields.Fact: In general 2f + 1 servers tolerate f failures.
fields.Source: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Question: What is the minimum cluster size for majority based consensus to survive one server failure?
fields.Fact: A 4 node cluster still tolerates only 1 failure, so even sizes add cost without adding tolerance.
fields.Source: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Question: In Raft, which state does every server start in?
fields.Fact: A follower becomes a candidate if it hears nothing from a leader before its election timeout.
fields.Source: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Question: In Raft, what is a server called while it is requesting votes to become leader?
fields.Fact: A candidate votes for itself and sends RequestVote RPCs to the others.
fields.Source: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Question: In Raft, which server accepts client requests and replicates log entries to the others?
fields.Hint: There is at most one per term.
fields.Fact: Raft sends all log entries through the leader, which simplifies reasoning about the log.
fields.Source: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Text: Raft divides time into numbered {{c1::terms}}, each beginning with an election.
fields.Extra: A server that sees a higher number steps down to follower.
fields.Hint: They act as a logical clock.
fields.Fact: A term may end with no leader if the vote is split.
fields.Source: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Text: Raft uses {{c1::randomized}} election timeouts so that split votes are rare and resolve quickly.
fields.Extra: The paper suggests timeouts such as 150 to 300 ms.
fields.Hint: Not every follower should wake up at the same moment.
fields.Fact: Randomization was chosen over a ranking scheme because it was simpler and worked well.
fields.Source: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Text: A Raft leader considers a log entry from its current term committed once it is stored on a {{c1::majority}} of servers.
fields.Extra: Committed entries are then applied to the state machine.
fields.Fact: Raft's paper notes leaders do not commit entries from earlier terms just by counting replicas.
fields.Source: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Question: What does a Raft leader send periodically, as empty AppendEntries calls, to keep followers from starting elections?
fields.Fact: Raft reuses the same RPC for both heartbeats and log replication.
fields.Source: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Text: Raft was designed with {{c1::understandability}} as its primary goal, compared with Paxos.
fields.Extra: Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout, 2014.
fields.Fact: The authors ran a user study where students learned Raft and Paxos and took quizzes on each.
fields.Source: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Side B: Votes on proposals and remembers the highest numbered proposal it has promised
fields.Hint: One of three Paxos roles, alongside proposer and learner.
fields.Fact: A value is chosen once a majority of acceptors have accepted it.

fields.Side B: Picks a proposal number and asks acceptors to promise and then accept a value
fields.Fact: Competing proposers can block each other indefinitely, which is why a distinguished leader is used in practice.

fields.Question: What is the first phase of single decree Paxos, where acceptors promise to ignore lower numbered proposals?
fields.Aliases:
Prepare and promise
Phase 1
Prepare phase
fields.Fact: Phase 2 is the accept phase.

fields.Text: Lamport's 2001 paper "{{c1::Paxos Made Simple}}" states that the algorithm, presented in plain English, is very simple.
fields.Extra: Published in 2001 after the original paper was widely seen as hard to read.
fields.Fact: The original Part-Time Parliament paper framed the algorithm as a fictional Greek parliament.

fields.Text: In {{c1::two phase commit}}, a coordinator asks all participants to prepare, then tells them all to commit or abort.
fields.Extra: If the coordinator fails after prepare, participants can be blocked.
fields.Fact: Two phase commit is an atomic commitment protocol and is not the same as consensus.

fields.Text: {{c1::Split brain}} happens when two nodes both believe they are leader and accept conflicting writes.
fields.Extra: Majority quorums and fencing tokens prevent it.
fields.Fact: A fencing token is a number that increases each time a lock or leadership is granted, so storage can reject stale leaders.

fields.Question: Which delivery guarantee means a message may be lost but is never delivered twice?
fields.Fact: Committing the consumer offset before processing gives this behaviour in Kafka.

fields.Question: Which delivery guarantee means a message is never lost but may be delivered more than once?
fields.Fact: It is safe only if consumers handle duplicates, usually by being idempotent.

fields.Question: Which delivery guarantee means each message affects the result one time, with no loss and no duplicates?
fields.Fact: In practice it is built from at least once delivery plus deduplication or transactions.

fields.Text: Kafka provides exactly once semantics for stream processing through the {{c1::idempotent producer}} and {{c2::transactions}}.
fields.Extra: Added in Kafka 0.11.
fields.Hint: Two features: one stops duplicate writes, one makes writes atomic.
fields.Fact: The guarantee covers reads and writes within Kafka; external side effects still need their own deduplication.

fields.Text: Kafka guarantees message order only within a single {{c1::partition}}.
fields.Extra: Messages with the same key go to the same partition by default.
fields.Fact: Choosing an order id or user id as the key keeps related events in sequence.

fields.Text: Within a Kafka {{c1::consumer group}}, each partition is consumed by exactly one member.
fields.Extra: So a topic's partition count caps the useful parallelism of one group.
fields.Hint: A set of consumers sharing the work.
fields.Fact: Extra consumers beyond the partition count sit idle.

fields.Text: A Kafka consumer tracks its position in each partition with an {{c1::offset}}.
fields.Extra: Committed offsets let a consumer resume after a restart.
fields.Hint: A number per message in the log.
fields.Fact: Kafka keeps messages for a retention period whether or not they were consumed.

fields.Side B: Each message is processed by one consumer
fields.Fact: Adding consumers to a queue raises throughput because they share the messages.

fields.Side B: Each message is delivered to every subscriber
fields.Fact: Kafka gives both models: one consumer group acts like a queue, several groups act like pub/sub.

fields.Question: Where do messages go after they fail processing too many times?
fields.Hint: A parking spot for poison messages.
fields.Fact: Amazon SQS moves a message to the DLQ after maxReceiveCount receives.

fields.Question: In Amazon SQS, what is the period during which a received message is hidden from other consumers?
fields.Hint: If you do not delete it in time, it reappears.
fields.Fact: The default visibility timeout in SQS is 30 seconds.

fields.Text: Amazon SQS standard queues provide {{c1::at least once}} delivery and best effort ordering.
fields.Extra: FIFO queues add ordering within a message group and deduplication.
fields.Fact: SQS FIFO deduplicates messages with the same deduplication id within a 5 minute interval.

fields.Text: {{c1::Backpressure}} is a signal from a slow consumer that makes producers slow down instead of overflowing buffers.
fields.Extra: Bounded queues are a simple form of it.
fields.Fact: Unbounded queues hide overload until memory runs out.

fields.Text: The {{c1::transactional outbox}} pattern writes an event to a table in the same database transaction as the business change, and a relay publishes it later.
fields.Extra: It avoids the dual write problem between a database and a broker.
fields.Hint: A box of outgoing mail in the same database.
fields.Fact: The relay can publish an event more than once, so consumers must still be idempotent.

fields.Text: A {{c1::saga}} is a sequence of local transactions where each failure triggers {{c2::compensating}} transactions to undo earlier steps.
fields.Extra: It replaces a distributed transaction across services.
fields.Fact: Sagas give up isolation: other transactions can see intermediate states.

fields.Text: {{c1::CQRS}} separates the model used to update data from the model used to read it.
fields.Extra: Command Query Responsibility Segregation.
fields.Fact: Read models in CQRS are often updated asynchronously, so they can lag behind writes.

fields.Text: An operation is {{c1::idempotent}} if performing it several times has the same effect as performing it once.
fields.Extra: This makes retries safe.
fields.Hint: Setting a value versus incrementing it.
fields.Fact: Setting x = 5 is idempotent; adding 1 to x is not.

fields.Question: Among the methods defined in RFC 9110, which one used to submit data for processing is not idempotent?
fields.Hint: It is the one used to create things.
fields.Fact: PATCH is also not guaranteed to be idempotent.

fields.Question: Which HTTP method replaces a resource with the request payload and is defined as idempotent?
fields.Fact: DELETE is idempotent too, even though the second call may return 404.

fields.Question: Which request header does Stripe use to make POST requests safe to retry?
fields.Hint: It names the property it gives.
fields.Fact: Stripe recommends a random V4 UUID or similar for the key value.

fields.Text: A server implements idempotency keys by storing the {{c1::response}} for each key and returning it for repeated requests with the same key.
fields.Extra: Keys are usually expired after a retention window.
fields.Hint: What does a retry get back?
fields.Fact: Stripe returns the same result for a repeated key, including errors.

fields.Text: With at least once delivery, a consumer can stay correct by recording processed {{c1::message ids}} and skipping duplicates.
fields.Extra: Store the id in the same transaction as the effect.
fields.Fact: Doing the side effect and recording the id in one transaction closes the crash window between them.

fields.Question: Which rate limiting algorithm refills tokens at a fixed rate and allows bursts up to the bucket capacity?
fields.Fact: Two parameters fully describe it: refill rate and capacity.

fields.Question: Which rate limiting algorithm drains a queue at a constant rate, smoothing bursts into a steady output?
fields.Hint: Water drips out of a hole at a constant rate.
fields.Fact: Requests that arrive when the bucket is full are dropped.

fields.Question: Which rate limiting algorithm counts requests per calendar interval, and can let up to twice the limit through around the boundary?
fields.Fact: A client can send the full limit at the end of one window and again at the start of the next.
fields.Source: How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains (https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/)

fields.Question: Which rate limiting algorithm stores a timestamp for every request and counts those within the last interval?
fields.Hint: Exact, but memory grows with traffic.
fields.Fact: Memory use grows with the number of requests allowed per window.
fields.Source: How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains (https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/)

fields.Question: Which rate limiting algorithm estimates the rate by weighting the previous window's count by how much of it overlaps the current interval?
fields.Hint: Two counters and a weighted average.
fields.Fact: Cloudflare described using this approximation to rate limit at very large scale.
fields.Source: How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains (https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/)

fields.Question: Which HTTP status code means Too Many Requests?
fields.Aliases:
429 Too Many Requests
Too Many Requests
fields.Fact: A 429 response may include Retry-After to tell the client how long to wait.

fields.Question: Which response header tells a client how long to wait before retrying?
fields.Hint: It can hold seconds or an HTTP date.
fields.Fact: It is used with 503 and 429 responses and with redirects.

fields.Text:
Fill in the refill step of a token bucket:
tokens = min(capacity, tokens + {{c1::rate * elapsed}})
if tokens >= 1:
    tokens -= 1
    allow()
fields.Extra: Tokens are added in proportion to time passed, capped at capacity.
fields.Hint: Refill depends on two things: speed and time.
fields.Fact: Lazy refill on each request avoids a background timer per bucket.

fields.Side B: Many small, low latency reads and writes of individual records
fields.Fact: OLTP databases usually store data row by row.

fields.Side B: Large scans and aggregations over many rows for analytics
fields.Fact: Analytical stores usually lay data out by column to scan less.

fields.Text: A {{c1::column oriented}} store keeps each column's values together, so queries that read few columns scan less data and compress well.
fields.Extra: Typical for data warehouses.
fields.Hint: Layout by attribute, not by record.
fields.Fact: Repeated values in a column compress well with run length or dictionary encoding.

fields.Question: Which index structure, used by most relational databases, keeps sorted keys in fixed size pages and updates them in place?
fields.Aliases:
B tree
Btree
B+ tree
B+tree
fields.Fact: A B-tree with a branching factor of 500 needs only four levels to address a very large table.

fields.Question: Which storage engine design buffers writes in memory, flushes them as sorted immutable files and merges them in the background?
fields.Aliases:
LSM-tree
Log-structured merge tree
Log structured merge tree
LSM
fields.Fact: The LSM tree was described by O'Neil and colleagues in 1996.

fields.Text: In an LSM engine, an in memory {{c1::memtable}} is flushed to disk as an immutable sorted file called an {{c2::SSTable}}.
fields.Extra: Background compaction merges SSTables and discards overwritten values.
fields.Fact: Bigtable's paper popularised the SSTable name.
fields.Source: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data (https://research.google/pubs/bigtable-a-distributed-storage-system-for-structured-data/)

fields.Text: A {{c1::write ahead log}} records changes durably before they are applied, so a crash can be recovered by replaying it.
fields.Extra: Also abbreviated WAL.
fields.Fact: LSM engines use a log to protect the memtable, since memory is lost in a crash.

fields.Text: Compared with B-trees, LSM trees usually offer higher {{c1::write}} throughput, while B-trees often give more predictable {{c2::read}} performance.
fields.Extra: LSM writes are sequential; reads may check several files.
fields.Hint: One engine favours one side of the workload.
fields.Fact: Compaction in LSM engines causes write amplification and can compete with live traffic for disk bandwidth.

fields.Question: Which kind of database stores opaque values looked up by a single key, like Redis or DynamoDB?
fields.Aliases:
Key value store
Key-value database
KV store
fields.Fact: Key-value stores trade query flexibility for simple, predictable lookups.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Question: Which kind of database, like Cassandra or Bigtable, stores rows with many dynamic columns grouped into families?
fields.Aliases:
Wide column store
Wide-column database
Column family store
fields.Fact: Bigtable describes itself as a sparse, distributed, persistent multidimensional sorted map.
fields.Source: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data (https://research.google/pubs/bigtable-a-distributed-storage-system-for-structured-data/)

fields.Question: Which kind of database stores self contained JSON like records, like MongoDB?
fields.Fact: Document models work well when data is read as a whole tree, such as a profile with nested items.

fields.Question: Which kind of database models data as vertices and edges and is suited to many to many relationships?
fields.Fact: Cypher, SPARQL and Gremlin are examples of graph query languages.

fields.Question: Which kind of storage, like Amazon S3, holds large binary blobs addressed by a key in a flat namespace?
fields.Aliases:
Object store
Blob storage
Blob store
fields.Hint: Images and videos usually live here.
fields.Fact: Systems usually store the blob in object storage and keep only its key in the database.

fields.Text: Since December 2020, Amazon S3 provides {{c1::strong read after write}} consistency for PUT and DELETE of objects.
fields.Extra: Before that, overwrites and deletes were eventually consistent.
fields.Fact: AWS made the change automatically at no extra cost.

fields.Text: ACID stands for Atomicity, {{c1::Consistency}}, {{c2::Isolation}} and Durability.
fields.Extra: The C is about application invariants, not the C in CAP.
fields.Fact: Theo Haerder and Andreas Reuter coined the acronym in 1983.

fields.Question: Which isolation level prevents dirty reads and is the default in PostgreSQL?
fields.Hint: You only see data that was committed.
fields.Fact: Each statement in PostgreSQL read committed sees a fresh snapshot.

fields.Question: Which SQL isolation level is the strongest, preventing every concurrency anomaly?
fields.Hint: As if transactions ran one at a time.
fields.Fact: PostgreSQL implements it with serializable snapshot isolation since version 9.1.

fields.Question: In PostgreSQL, which isolation level gives each transaction one snapshot taken at its first statement?
fields.Hint: Re-reading the same row returns the same value.
fields.Fact: PostgreSQL repeatable read does not allow phantom reads, which is stricter than the SQL standard requires.

fields.Text: {{c1::Write skew}} happens when two transactions read the same data, then update different rows based on it, breaking an invariant.
fields.Extra: Snapshot isolation allows it; serializable isolation prevents it.
fields.Hint: Two doctors both go off call at once.
fields.Fact: The on call doctors example is a classic illustration from Designing Data-Intensive Applications.

fields.Side B: All writes go to one node, which streams changes to followers
fields.Aliases:
Leader follower replication
Primary replica replication
Master slave replication
fields.Fact: It avoids write conflicts, but the leader caps write throughput.

fields.Side B: Clients send writes to several replicas and use quorums for reads and writes
fields.Fact: Cassandra and Riak follow this model, inspired by Dynamo.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Side B: Several nodes accept writes and replicate to each other, so conflicts must be resolved
fields.Aliases:
Multi leader replication
Multi-master replication
Active active
fields.Fact: It is often used across datacenters so each region can accept local writes.

fields.Text: {{c1::Last write wins}} resolves conflicts by keeping the value with the highest timestamp and silently discarding the others.
fields.Extra: Simple but can lose data, and clock skew makes it worse.
fields.Fact: Cassandra uses last write wins at the cell level.

fields.Text: {{c1::Denormalization}} copies data into several places to avoid joins at read time, at the cost of more complex writes.
fields.Extra: Common in read heavy and NoSQL designs.
fields.Fact: Every copy must be updated when the source changes, or it goes stale.

fields.Text: In a sharded database, a {{c1::global}} secondary index is partitioned by the indexed value, while a {{c2::local}} one lives on each shard beside its data.
fields.Extra: Local indexes make reads scatter to all shards; global indexes make writes touch several shards.
fields.Fact: Global indexes are often updated asynchronously, so they can briefly lag the data.

fields.Text: {{c1::HyperLogLog}} estimates the number of distinct items using a small, fixed amount of memory.
fields.Extra: Redis implements it with PFADD and PFCOUNT.
fields.Fact: The PF prefix in Redis commands honours Philippe Flajolet.
fields.Source: HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm (https://algo.inria.fr/flajolet/Publications/FlFuGaMe07.pdf)

fields.Question: In Norvig's latency table, roughly how long is an L1 cache reference?
fields.Fact: These figures are approximate and date from the 2000s, but the ratios are what matter.
fields.Source: Teach Yourself Programming in Ten Years (https://norvig.com/21-days.html)

fields.Question: In Norvig's latency table, roughly how long is a main memory reference?
fields.Hint: About two hundred times an L1 hit.
fields.Fact: A memory reference is about 200 times slower than an L1 cache hit in the table.
fields.Source: Teach Yourself Programming in Ten Years (https://norvig.com/21-days.html)

fields.Question: In Norvig's latency table, roughly how long is a round trip within the same datacenter?
fields.Fact: Listed as 500,000 nanoseconds.
fields.Source: Teach Yourself Programming in Ten Years (https://norvig.com/21-days.html)

fields.Question: In Norvig's latency table, roughly how long does a disk seek take?
fields.Fact: A disk seek costs about as much as 16 datacenter round trips in that table.
fields.Source: Teach Yourself Programming in Ten Years (https://norvig.com/21-days.html)

fields.Question: In Norvig's latency table, roughly how long does a packet take to go from the US to Europe and back?
fields.Hint: Bounded by the speed of light in fibre.
fields.Fact: No amount of server tuning removes this delay; only moving data closer to users does.
fields.Source: Teach Yourself Programming in Ten Years (https://norvig.com/21-days.html)

fields.Question: Which is faster to read 1 MB sequentially from, according to Norvig's table: memory or spinning disk?
fields.Hint: Think of electronics versus moving parts.
fields.Fact: In the table, reading 1 MB from memory is about 80 times faster than from disk.
fields.Source: Teach Yourself Programming in Ten Years (https://norvig.com/21-days.html)

fields.Text: In Norvig's table, reading 1 MB sequentially from memory takes about {{c1::250 microseconds}}, and from disk about {{c2::20 milliseconds}}.
fields.Extra: Listed as 250,000 ns and 20,000,000 ns.
fields.Hint: The disk figure is in milliseconds.
fields.Fact: Sequential disk reads are far faster than random reads because they avoid seeks.
fields.Source: Teach Yourself Programming in Ten Years (https://norvig.com/21-days.html)

fields.Text: Light in optical fibre travels at roughly {{c1::two thirds}} of its speed in a vacuum, about 200,000 km per second.
fields.Extra: So 1,000 km of fibre adds about 5 ms each way.
fields.Hint: The refractive index of glass is about 1.5.
fields.Fact: Real paths add delay because fibre rarely follows the great circle route.

fields.Question: How many seconds are in a day?
fields.Fact: Rounding a day to 100,000 seconds makes mental math easier and errs on the safe side.

fields.Question: About how many requests per second is 1 million requests per day, on average?
fields.Hint: Divide by the seconds in a day.
fields.Fact: Peak traffic is often several times the daily average, so size for the peak.

fields.Question: About how many requests per second is 100 million requests per day, on average?
fields.Hint: About a hundred times the 1 million per day figure.
fields.Fact: 100,000,000 divided by 86,400 is about 1,157.

fields.Question: What is 2 to the power of 10?
fields.Fact: This is why a kibibyte is 1,024 bytes.

fields.Question: 2 to the power of 30 is roughly how many?
fields.Hint: Three factors of about a thousand.
fields.Fact: Exactly, it is 1,073,741,824, one gibibyte in bytes.

fields.Question: Roughly how many distinct values fit in an unsigned 32 bit integer?
fields.Fact: Running out of 32 bit ids is a real failure mode for fast growing tables.

fields.Question: About how much downtime per year does 99.9% availability allow?
fields.Aliases:
8.8 hours
8.76 h
8.77 hours
9 hours
about 9 hours
fields.Fact: The Google SRE book lists 8.76 hours per year for 99.9%.

fields.Question: About how much downtime per year does 99.99% availability allow?
fields.Fact: Each extra nine divides the allowed downtime by ten.

fields.Question: About how much downtime per year does 99.999% availability allow?
fields.Fact: At five nines, a single slow manual recovery can use the whole year's budget.

fields.Text: If a request depends on two services in series, each 99.9% available, the combined availability is about {{c1::99.8%}}.
fields.Extra: Multiply the availabilities: 0.999 times 0.999.
fields.Hint: Dependencies multiply, they do not average.
fields.Fact: This is why deep call chains need each dependency to be more available than the whole service.

fields.Text: Storing 1 KB for each of 1 million new records per day needs about {{c1::1 GB}} per day, or roughly 365 GB per year.
fields.Extra: Ignoring replication and indexes.
fields.Fact: Replication by a factor of three triples the raw estimate.

fields.Text: The Google SRE book's four golden signals are latency, {{c1::traffic}}, {{c2::errors}} and {{c3::saturation}}.
fields.Extra: If you can measure only four metrics of a user facing system, measure these.
fields.Hint: One is about how full the service is.
fields.Fact: The SRE book advises distinguishing the latency of successful requests from that of failed ones.
fields.Source: Site Reliability Engineering: Monitoring Distributed Systems (https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/)

fields.Text: The RED method for request driven services tracks {{c1::Rate}}, {{c2::Errors}} and {{c3::Duration}}.
fields.Extra: Proposed by Tom Wilkie.
fields.Fact: RED covers three of the four golden signals, leaving out saturation.
fields.Source: The RED Method: key metrics for microservices architecture (https://grafana.com/blog/2018/08/02/the-red-method-how-to-instrument-your-services/)

fields.Text: Brendan Gregg's USE method checks every resource for {{c1::Utilization}}, {{c2::Saturation}} and {{c3::Errors}}.
fields.Extra: Resources include CPUs, disks, memory and network interfaces.
fields.Fact: The method is meant to find bottlenecks quickly with a checklist rather than guesswork.

fields.Side B: A measured indicator of service level, such as the fraction of requests served under 300 ms
fields.Fact: Good SLIs reflect what users experience, not internal resource metrics.
fields.Source: Site Reliability Engineering: Service Level Objectives (https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)

fields.Side B: A target value or range for an SLI, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding
fields.Fact: An SLO that is too strict slows down shipping without users noticing the difference.
fields.Source: Site Reliability Engineering: Service Level Objectives (https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)

fields.Side B: A contract with users that specifies consequences, such as refunds, if objectives are missed
fields.Fact: The SRE book notes that SLAs are closely tied to business and product decisions.
fields.Source: Site Reliability Engineering: Service Level Objectives (https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)

fields.Text: An {{c1::error budget}} is the amount of unreliability an SLO allows, such as 0.1% of requests for a 99.9% target.
fields.Extra: Teams can spend it on risky launches; when it runs out, they slow down.
fields.Fact: Error budgets turn reliability versus velocity debates into a number both sides can agree on.
fields.Source: Site Reliability Engineering: Service Level Objectives (https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)

fields.Text: Report latency as percentiles such as p99, because the {{c1::mean}} hides slow outliers.
fields.Extra: A p99 of 800 ms means 1% of requests take longer than 800 ms.
fields.Fact: When one page load fans out to many backends, the slowest backend often sets the page's latency.
fields.Source: Site Reliability Engineering: Monitoring Distributed Systems (https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/)

fields.Text: You cannot average p99 values from several servers to get the fleet p99; aggregate {{c1::histograms}} instead.
fields.Extra: Sum bucket counts, then compute the percentile.
fields.Hint: Merge the distributions, not the summaries.
fields.Fact: Fixed bucket histograms trade some precision for being cheap to merge.

fields.Side B: Records the path of one request across services as a tree of timed spans
fields.Hint: Follows a single request end to end.
fields.Fact: OpenTelemetry treats traces, metrics and logs as its core signals.

fields.Side B: A numeric measurement aggregated over time, such as requests per second
fields.Hint: Cheap to store, good for dashboards and alerts.
fields.Fact: Metrics are cheap because they aggregate, but that also discards per request detail.

fields.Side B: A timestamped record of a discrete event, often structured as key value pairs
fields.Fact: Structured logs in JSON are far easier to query than free text.

fields.Question: In distributed tracing, what is a single timed unit of work, such as one RPC, called?
fields.Hint: Traces are built from many of these.
fields.Fact: Each one carries a trace id shared by all of them in the request and its own id.

fields.Question: Which HTTP header does W3C Trace Context use to propagate trace and parent span ids?
fields.Fact: A companion header, tracestate, carries vendor specific data.

fields.Text: Using user ids as metric labels creates high {{c1::cardinality}}: one time series per unique label combination.
fields.Extra: This can overwhelm a metrics backend.
fields.Fact: Put per user detail in logs or traces, and keep metric labels bounded.

fields.Text: The SRE book recommends paging on {{c1::symptoms}} users feel, such as errors and latency, rather than on every possible cause.
fields.Extra: Causes still help with debugging dashboards.
fields.Fact: Pages that require no action train people to ignore pages.
fields.Source: Site Reliability Engineering: Monitoring Distributed Systems (https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/)

fields.Side B: Tests externally visible behaviour as a user would see it
fields.Fact: The SRE book pairs it with white box monitoring based on internal metrics.
fields.Source: Site Reliability Engineering: Monitoring Distributed Systems (https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/)

fields.Question: How many characters does base62 encoding use?
fields.Fact: 26 lowercase letters plus 26 uppercase plus 10 digits.
fields.Source: RFC 3986: Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986)

fields.Text: Base62 is popular for short links because letters and digits are {{c1::unreserved}} URI characters that never need percent encoding.
fields.Extra: RFC 3986 unreserved characters also include hyphen, period, underscore and tilde.
fields.Hint: Safe to put in a URL as is.
fields.Fact: Base64's plus and slash characters would need escaping in a URL path.
fields.Source: RFC 3986: Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986)

fields.Question: Roughly how many distinct codes do 7 base62 characters give?
fields.Fact: At 1,000 new links per second, that space would last over a century.
fields.Source: RFC 3986: Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986)

fields.Question: Which redirect status code is permanent and cacheable by browsers by default, reducing load but hiding repeat clicks from a shortener's analytics?
fields.Fact: Browsers may cache it and skip the shortener on later visits.

fields.Question: Which redirect status code is temporary, so browsers keep asking the shortener and every click can be counted?
fields.Hint: The temporary one from HTTP/1.0 days.
fields.Fact: 307 is similar but guarantees the method is not changed.

fields.Question: Which redirect status code is permanent and also guarantees the request method is kept?
fields.Fact: It was added later than 301 to fix method changes on POST.

fields.Text: A URL shortener can avoid collision checks by encoding a unique {{c1::numeric id}} in base62 instead of hashing the long URL.
fields.Extra: Hash truncation needs collision handling.
fields.Hint: Turn a counter into a code.
fields.Fact: Sequential ids make codes guessable, so some services shuffle or encrypt the id first.

fields.Text: URL shorteners are usually {{c1::read heavy}}, so a cache in front of the code to URL mapping absorbs most traffic.
fields.Extra: Popular links follow a long tail distribution.
fields.Fact: Because mappings rarely change, they cache very well.

fields.Text: Twitter's Snowflake ids are 64 bits: a {{c1::timestamp}}, a worker id and a per worker {{c2::sequence}} number.
fields.Extra: 41 bits of milliseconds, 10 bits of worker id, 12 bits of sequence.
fields.Hint: Time first, so ids sort roughly by creation.
fields.Fact: Each worker can generate up to 4,096 ids per millisecond.

fields.Question: Which 128 bit id scheme needs no coordination at all but produces ids that are random and not time ordered in its version 4?
fields.Fact: Random keys scatter inserts across a B-tree index, which hurts write locality.

fields.Side B: Push each new post into every follower's feed cache when it is created
fields.Aliases:
Push model
Fan out on write
fields.Fact: Fast feed reads, but a celebrity post means millions of writes.

fields.Side B: Build a feed when it is requested by merging recent posts from everyone the user follows
fields.Aliases:
Pull model
Fan out on read
fields.Fact: Cheap posting, but every feed load queries many timelines.

fields.Text: Feeds often use a {{c1::hybrid}} approach: push posts from most accounts, but pull posts from celebrities with huge follower counts at read time.
fields.Extra: DDIA describes Twitter moving toward this approach.
fields.Fact: The split avoids millions of writes for each post by a very popular account.

fields.Text: Feeds use {{c1::cursor}} based pagination rather than offsets, so new items at the top do not shift or duplicate pages.
fields.Extra: The cursor encodes the last seen item, for example its id or timestamp.
fields.Fact: Large offsets are also slow, because the database still walks past the skipped rows.

fields.Text: Chat servers commonly use {{c1::WebSockets}}, which give a full duplex connection over a single TCP connection.
fields.Extra: Standardised in RFC 6455.
fields.Hint: It starts as an HTTP Upgrade.
fields.Fact: The WebSocket handshake uses the HTTP Upgrade mechanism with a 101 Switching Protocols response.

fields.Side B: The client sends a request that the server holds open until new data arrives or a timeout fires
fields.Fact: It works over plain HTTP but costs a new request after each message.

fields.Question: Which HTTP status code does a server send to accept a WebSocket upgrade?
fields.Hint: It is in the 1xx informational class.
fields.Fact: The client proves it speaks WebSocket by sending a Sec-WebSocket-Key header.

fields.Text: Chat systems order messages within a conversation using a per conversation {{c1::sequence number}} rather than client clocks.
fields.Extra: Client clocks can be wrong or skewed.
fields.Hint: A counter scoped to each chat.
fields.Fact: Ordering is usually only needed within a conversation, which keeps the problem partitionable.
fields.Source: Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System (https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/time-clocks.pdf)

fields.Text: Online presence is usually tracked with periodic {{c1::heartbeats}}, marking a user offline when they stop arriving.
fields.Extra: A short grace period avoids flapping on brief network drops.
fields.Hint: Regular signs of life from the client.
fields.Fact: Presence updates are often batched or rate limited because they fan out to every contact.

fields.Text: When a chat recipient is offline, the server stores the message and sends a {{c1::push notification}} through the platform service.
fields.Extra: Apple Push Notification service and Firebase Cloud Messaging are common.
fields.Fact: The message is delivered over the live connection once the client reconnects.

fields.Text: Chat history is often stored in a wide-column store keyed by {{c1::conversation id}} with messages sorted by sequence.
fields.Extra: This makes loading recent messages a single partition range read.
fields.Hint: Partition by the chat, sort by time.
fields.Fact: Discord has written about storing messages in Cassandra and later ScyllaDB partitioned by channel and time bucket.
fields.Source: How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages (https://discord.com/blog/how-discord-stores-trillions-of-messages)

fields.Text: Clients attach a unique {{c1::client message id}} to each sent message so retries over flaky networks do not create duplicates.
fields.Extra: The server deduplicates on that id.
fields.Hint: Same idea as an idempotency key.
fields.Fact: This lets the client safely resend after a timeout without knowing whether the first send succeeded.

fields.Text: {{c1::GeoDNS}} answers DNS queries with different addresses depending on the resolver's location, sending users to a nearby region.
fields.Extra: DNS answers are cached for their TTL, so failover is not instant.
fields.Fact: EDNS Client Subnet lets resolvers pass part of the client address so the answer can be more precise.
fields.Source: RFC 7871: Client Subnet in DNS Queries (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7871)
